note.note:
History:
- Chief complaint: Upper lip swelling (started at left corner, now generalized to upper lip) after eating prawn soup.
- Onset/timing: Ate prawn soup ~7 PM; swelling began ~30 minutes later.
- Progression: Worsening; feels like “pumping blood” and increasing size.
- Associated symptoms: Difficulty breathing/feeling throat tight; possible chest tightness (patient unsure); dizziness.
- Triggers/context: First time trying prawn soup at a restaurant; previously chooses vegetarian options.
- Prior episodes: ~1 year ago after late-night Chinese/curry; woke with facial swelling and difficulty breathing. Childhood severe allergic reaction to peanuts reportedly required an injection and hospital visit (per mother; patient uncertain on details).

Past Medical History:
- Asthma.
- Allergies: Peanut allergy (longstanding; reportedly severe in childhood). Shellfish allergy not previously diagnosed.
- Medications:
  - Salbutamol inhaler (dose/route/frequency not documented); used regularly.
  - Antihistamines used “sometimes” for peanut allergy (specific agent/dose/frequency not documented); none available initially during this event.
- No additional chronic conditions, surgeries, or hospitalizations documented beyond childhood reaction (details unclear).

Physical Examination:
- Patient-reported findings during teleconsultation:
  - Upper lip swelling, progressive.
  - Subjective dyspnea; feels throat may be closing.
  - Possible chest tightness (uncertain).
  - Dizziness.
- No rash, hives, wheeze, stridor, tongue swelling, GI symptoms, or syncope reported.
- No objective vitals or in-person exam performed/documented.

Impression:
- Suspected anaphylactic reaction following ingestion of prawn soup in a patient with peanut allergy and asthma.

Management Plan:
- Emergency action: Advised immediate ambulance activation (999) for suspected anaphylaxis; instructed patient to remain with another person until EMS arrival.
- Interim measure: Take available antihistamine while awaiting ambulance.
- Post-ED care: After hospital discharge, instructed to contact clinic for follow-up to “sort out injections and things like that” (specific medication/device not documented).
- Safety: Keep companion present until EMS arrives; monitor for worsening breathing.

Patient Summary:
- Maria developed rapidly progressive lip swelling, dyspnea, and dizziness within 30 minutes of eating prawn soup. Given history of severe peanut allergy and prior similar episode, this was treated as suspected anaphylaxis. She was directed to call 999, take an antihistamine while waiting, and arrange follow-up after hospital care for further management.

Key Takeaways:
- Call 999 immediately for suspected anaphylaxis and do not delay.
- Take an antihistamine while awaiting the ambulance and stay with someone.
- Contact the clinic after hospital discharge to arrange further treatment, including injections (details not documented).

Next Steps:
- Emergency department evaluation and management via ambulance.
- Post-hospital follow-up with clinic to arrange ongoing anaphylaxis management and prescription of “injections” as referenced (specific agent/device not documented).

Quality checks:
- Missing expected elements: Vitals, objective exam (airway, breathing, circulation), detailed allergy history (exact prior reactions, specific triggers), current medication list reconciliation with doses/routes/frequencies, documentation of any epinephrine auto-injector possession or use, past hospital records.
- Internal conflicts: Initial presenting food described as “sandwich” in notes vs. patient clarifies prawn soup; chest tightness reported as uncertain.
- Transcript quality: Understandable but conversational; some uncertainty and interruptions; limited objective detail due to teleconsult and acute distress.
